summary: A 16-qubit superconducting processor implements Mach–Zehnder interferometry on 4 and 12 qubits to demonstrate the wave-to-particle transition controlled by which-way measurement strength and observe the quantum Zeno effect under continuous measurement. Quantum state tomography reveals complementarity relations: $2(1-P_s)+V^2 \leq 1$ (purity-visibility) and $S_s \leq S_s^\mathrm{sym}(V)$ (von Neumann entropy-visibility), connecting wave-particle duality to quantum information leakage.
motivation: Superconducting qubits enable tunable which-way measurements via QND dispersive readout without destroying the photon, permitting systematic exploration of Bohr complementarity from weak to projective measurement regimes and investigation of information leakage during the wave-particle transition.
method: A 4-qubit interferometer with decoupled which-way measurement and a 12-qubit interferometer with continuous measurement both map photon propagation onto qubit populations via the hard-core-boson Hamiltonian; measurement-induced dephasing rates $\Gamma_m/2\pi$ are calibrated from Stark shifts and state tomography, visibility $V$ extracted from interference fringes, and two-qubit concurrence, purity $P_s$, and entropy $S_s$ computed from density matrices of qubits in the two arms.
result: Visibility decreases monotonically with $\Gamma_m$ from near unity to zero; concurrence drops from $\approx 0.717$ to $\approx 0$; the 12-qubit case shows nonmonotonic purity (minimum) and entropy (maximum) due to quantum Zeno blocking of path 2 when $\Gamma_m$ exceeds the nearest-neighbor hopping rate $J/2\pi \approx 3.56$ MHz, identifying optimal measurement strength for time-of-arrival protocols.
